tagline: Kirat Rai temple on a ridge above Aritar
meta_description: Mankhim, Aritar, Sikkim: the Kirat Rai temple at about 1,980 m, the Sakewa festival, views and respectful visiting tips, plus how to reach it and costs.
summary: Mankhim, also written Mangkhim, is the temple of the Kirat Rai community on a ridge at about 1,980 m above Aritar in Pakyong district. In the Rai language mang means deity and khim means house. The Rai gather here twice a year for Sakewa. It is a place of worship first and a viewpoint second.
intro: Mankhim stands on a ridge above Aritar, around 1,980 m above sea level, at a spot Wikipedia's Aritar article places at a village called Maity or Kheselakha. It is a temple of the Kirat Rai, one of the Kirati peoples of Sikkim, Nepal and the Darjeeling hills. The name is Rai: mang means deity and khim means house, as Wikipedia's article on Mankhim records.

The temple is reached by a road that climbs about 30 minutes from Aritar lake, followed by a short walk from the roadside to the top. From the ridge, Lampokhari looks like a drawn line below, the Rangpo valley falls away to the south, and on clear mornings the snow peaks stand on the north-west horizon. Sunrise is the best hour, and many Aritar homestays arrange early drives.

Most days Mankhim is quiet. Twice a year, in spring and again in late autumn, the Rai community gather here for Sakewa, the festival of the earth. Come as a guest: ask before photographing rituals, do not walk through dancers, and follow the guidance of local volunteers. Check current status and festival dates before you travel.

story.title: Sakewa and the Mundhum
story.text: Wikipedia's article on Mankhim records that the Rai community assembles at the temple twice a year for Sakewa, usually in April or May. Sakewa, also written Sakela, is described by Wikipedia as a festival of the Khambu Rai, and is tied to the Kirat year, which has two halves: Ubhauli, the going up, in spring, and Udhauli, the coming down, in the late year. The Rai ritual tradition is carried in the Mundhum, the oral scripture of the Kirat peoples, which Wikipedia describes as a body of teachings passed down through recitation. At Sakewa, a ritual leader, called a nakchhong in Rai tradition, recites verses while dancers circle to drums and cymbals. Many steps imitate farm work or animals. The festival is worship of the earth, asking for good harvests and protection. Visitors are welcome as guests when invited by local custom, but the ceremonies belong to the community, and nobody should treat them as a performance.
story.source: Wikipedia: Mankhim; Wikipedia: Sakela; Wikipedia: Mundhum

little_known.fact: Wikipedia gives Mankhim's height as about 6,500 ft, or roughly 1,980 m, and says it is in Maity village, also written Kheselakha, in the Aritar area.
Mankhim is one of six villages named for forest eco-development committees around Pangolakha Wildlife Sanctuary, along with Dalepchand, Lingtam, Phadamchen, Zuluk and Gnathang.
Wikipedia says the Rai assemble at Mankhim twice a year for Sakewa, with the spring gathering usually falling in April or May.

highlights.title: The Kirat Rai temple
highlights.text: A simple place of worship for the Rai community, set on the top of the ridge. Visit quietly, remove shoes, and ask a local before photographing the shrine or any ceremony in progress.

highlights.title: Sunrise from the ridge
highlights.text: Leave Aritar around 5 am in season. On clear mornings you see the Kangchenjunga range to the north-west and the Rangpo valley below. Cloud often rolls in by 8 am, so go early and carry a jacket.

highlights.title: Sakewa festival
highlights.text: In April or May the Rai gather here for the earth festival, with dance, drums and recitation. Dates follow a lunar calendar and a second gathering is held in late autumn. Check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: Forest road from Aritar
highlights.text: The drive up passes cardamom plots and mixed forest in about 30 minutes. You can walk down to Aritar village through forest and fields in 2 to 3 hours with a local guide.

highlights.title: Mankhim hill homestays
highlights.text: A few homestays stand near the temple at about 1,900–2,000 m, with the widest views in the area. Rooms are simple and nights are cooler than at the lake.

how_to_reach.text: There is no regular shared service to the temple. Take a shared jeep from Gangtok or Siliguri to Rhenock or Aritar, then hire a local car for the 30 minute climb, about ₹800–1,500 return including waiting. Ask your homestay to arrange it.

From Gangtok it is about 75 km and 3.5 hours via Pakyong, Rorathang and Aritar. The last section is narrow and steep, so a driver who knows it matters. A reserved small car from Gangtok costs about ₹4,000–5,500 for a day.

About 115–120 km and 4.5–5 hours via Rangpo, Rorathang and Aritar. NH10 can close after monsoon slides, and the alternative is via Kalimpong and Pedong. Pakyong Airport has no scheduled flights, so plan on Bagdogra (IXB) or NJP.

where_to_stay: Mankhim hill homestays sit near the temple at about 1,900–2,000 m, with the widest views and cooler nights; our mankhim-hill-homestays listing describes them. Aritar's lakeside homestays at about 1,450 m are more convenient for first-timers, and Lampokhari Village Resort is the more comfortable option. If you want a sunrise at the temple, stay the night before on the hill or at the lake and leave around 5 am. Book ahead around Sakewa, when families visit.
tips: Treat the temple as a place of worship: shoes off, voices low, ask before photographing.
Leave Aritar by 5 am for sunrise; clouds often cover the peaks by 8 am.
Carry a jacket, because the ridge is windy and cooler than the lake.
If you walk down, take a local guide, because forest paths branch and are slippery after rain.
Confirm Sakewa dates with your host and check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Sunrise at Mankhim ridge
experiences.summary: An early drive from Aritar to the ridge, timed for first light on the snow peaks and the valley below. The temple is the destination, and the view is the reward.
body: Leave your Aritar homestay around 5 am in season. The road climbs for about 30 minutes through forest and cardamom plots, and the final stretch is a short walk. Dress warmly: the ridge is windier and cooler than the lake, even in spring.

On a clear morning, the Kangchenjunga range shows to the north-west and the Rangpo valley drops to the south. Lampokhari lies like a pencil line below. By 8 am cloud often rises from the valleys, so the best light is brief.
Treat the temple as a place of worship, not a backdrop. Remove shoes, keep to quiet voices and ask a local before photographing the shrine. Do not climb on the structure or leave litter.

faqs.q: What time should we leave for sunrise?
faqs.a: Around 5 am in October to March and a bit earlier from April, when dawn is sooner. Allow 30 minutes for the drive and 10 minutes for the walk. Check the sunrise time for your date and ask your driver to confirm. Carry a torch.

faqs.q: Is the temple open to visitors?
faqs.a: Yes, during daylight, as a place of worship that people visit quietly. There is no fixed fee, and a small donation is welcome. Ceremonies may be in progress; ask before taking photographs. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Will we see Kangchenjunga for sure?
faqs.a: No. Clear mornings are most likely from October to December and in March and April, but cloud can hide the peaks on any day. If it is cloudy, you still get the valley and the quiet. We do not promise views.

experiences.title: Visiting Sakewa as a guest
experiences.summary: A respectful visit to Mankhim during Sakewa, when the Rai gather for the earth festival. You watch dance and listen to recitation as a guest of the community.
body: Sakewa is the main festival of the Khambu Rai, according to Wikipedia, and falls around the Baisakh full moon in spring, with a second gathering in late autumn. At Mankhim, the Rai community gather twice a year. The exact day follows the lunar calendar, so ask locally and check current status before you travel.

The ceremony includes recitation by a ritual leader and circle dances to drums and cymbals. Many movements mirror farm work and animals. Dress in modest, comfortable clothes, stand where volunteers direct you and never step into a dance circle uninvited.

Ask before photographing people, especially during rituals, and offer to share pictures. Do not use drones. Buy a snack or tea from local stalls if they are open, and avoid asking performers to repeat steps. The festival belongs to the community, and you attend as a guest.

faqs.a: The spring Sakewa falls around the Baisakh full moon, usually April or May, and a second gathering is held in late autumn. The exact day changes each year. Ask your homestay or the local committee and check current status before you travel.

Often yes, but ask first. Some rituals are private, and individuals may refuse. Do not use flash during recitation and do not block dancers. Offer to share photos. Never fly a drone over the gathering.

faqs.q: Do we need to book a stay for the festival?
faqs.a: Yes, book early. Homestays near Mankhim and Aritar fill with families on festival days. Confirm the dates with your host, because lunar dates shift each year, and ask about transport, since the road up is narrow and parking is limited.

experiences.title: Forest walk from Mankhim down to Aritar
experiences.image_query: Forest path Sikkim hills village walk
experiences.summary: A downhill walk through forest, cardamom plots and farm lanes from the temple ridge to Aritar, with a local guide, avoiding the road's hairpins.
body: Paths from Mankhim to Aritar cut across hairpins and run through mixed forest, farm terraces and cardamom shade. A local guide is worth the few hundred rupees: junctions are unmarked and paths change with landslides.

The walk takes about 2 to 3 hours downhill and is steep in places. Wear shoes with grip, carry water and a rain jacket, and start by 9 am. In the monsoon, leeches and slippery earth make it a poor idea.

The forest here is part of the wider Pangolakha landscape, where Wikipedia lists bird species such as laughingthrushes, minlas and yuhinas. Walk quietly and early for the best chances. We never promise any particular animal sighting.

faqs.a: It is a steep descent of 2 to 3 hours on earth and stone steps, with slippery sections after rain. Reasonable fitness and good shoes are enough, but seniors may prefer to ride down. Take a local guide and avoid the monsoon.

Yes, we advise one. Paths branch through forest and farmland, and landslides can change routes. A guide costs about ₹300–600 for a half day. Your homestay can arrange this. Agree the price before you set off.

Water, a rain jacket, a hat, snacks, shoes with grip and a charged phone, though signal can be weak. Bring a small bag for your litter. In the monsoon add leech socks. Ask your host about current trail conditions.

experiences.title: Hill homestay evening near Mankhim
experiences.image_query: Sikkim homestay kitchen dal bhat dinner
experiences.summary: An evening at a Mankhim hill homestay: dinner cooked at home, tea on the veranda and a quiet night above the lake, with cool air and wide views at first light.
body: Mankhim hill homestays are family homes that take guests, so evenings follow family rhythms. Arrive by late afternoon, have tea and walk to the temple ridge before dusk if the weather is clear.

Dinner is usually rice, dal, seasonal greens, a vegetable dish and either chicken or pork, or a vegetarian alternative on request. Ask what is growing in the garden that month. Fermented foods such as gundruk and pickles often appear, and large cardamom may flavour tea.

Nights are cooler than at the lake, so carry a fleece and expect thick quilts. Electricity and hot water can be limited, and signal is patchy. Book ahead and confirm what is included before you travel.

faqs.a: Home-style Sikkimese and Nepali food: rice, dal, vegetables, greens, a meat or egg dish, pickles and tea. Vegetarian meals are easy. Tell your host about allergies and preferences in advance, and ask for less chilli if needed.
Usually yes, from a geyser or bucket heated on request, but supply can be limited and electricity can fail. Ask when you book. Bring warm layers because nights are cool, and keep a torch handy.

faqs.q: How do we book a homestay at Mankhim?
faqs.a: Book through us or contact a homestay directly well ahead, especially around Sakewa and long weekends. Confirm room type, bathroom, meals, price and the road in. Pay the ₹50 entry fee collected at check-in. Check current status before you travel.

Mankhim, also written Mangkhim, is a Kirat Rai temple at about 1,980 m on a ridge above Aritar in Pakyong district. Wikipedia says mang means deity and khim means house in Rai. The community gathers here twice a year for Sakewa.

Yes, tourists can visit during daylight as guests. It is a working place of worship, so remove shoes, keep quiet and ask before photographing. Access during ceremonies may be limited. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Mankhim from Aritar?
faqs.a: About 30 minutes by car from Aritar lake, then a short walk from the road to the top. A walk down through forest takes 2 to 3 hours with a guide. Roads are narrow, so take a local driver.

The spring festival falls around the Baisakh full moon, usually April or May, with a second gathering in late autumn. Dates are lunar and change each year. Ask locally and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Mankhim?
faqs.a: No. Mankhim is in the Aritar area, outside the Silk Route protected area, so there is no special permit. Sikkim's ₹50 per tourist entry fee is collected by hotels at check-in. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a fee to enter the temple?
faqs.a: There is no fixed fee that we know of. A small donation is welcome. Parking or access charges may apply on festival days. Ask your driver or homestay before you go and check current status before you travel.

Often, but always ask first. Some rituals are private, and some people do not want to be photographed. Avoid flash and drones, never block dancers and offer to share pictures. Follow the instructions of local volunteers.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to visit?
faqs.a: Sunrise, around 5:30 to 7 am depending on season, when the peaks may be clear and the ridge is quiet. Cloud often covers the view by 8 am. Late afternoon is also pleasant, but views are less reliable.

The temple is reachable by car with a short walk from the road, which many seniors manage slowly. Steps and paths may be uneven. The walk down through forest is not suitable for most seniors. Ask your host about the walk before you go.
